plan.chapterName: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 14.3.10
plan.contextChunk: This figure is part of a worked example asking to evaluate the polar double integral of sin theta over the region R in the first quadrant outside the circle r = 2 and inside the cardioid r = 2(1 + cos theta). The figure shows both curves in polar coordinates: the circle r = 2 (blue) centered at the origin and the cardioid r = 2(1 + cos theta) (purple), which extends further to the right. The shaded region R (light blue) lies in the first quadrant between theta = 0 and theta = pi/2, bounded on the inside by the circle and on the outside by the cardioid; a red radial line at an intermediate angle shows a representative radial strip. The figure establishes the geometry of the integration region R needed to set up the polar iterated integral with inner limits from r = 2 to r = 2(1 + cos theta) and outer limits from theta = 0 to theta = pi/2.

interactionPlan.concept: In polar coordinates a region can be described by sweeping θ and letting r run from an inner boundary curve to an outer boundary curve, which is exactly what sets up the iterated integral ∫∫ f r dr dθ.
elements: horizontal polar axis (θ = 0 ray) drawn as a full black line through the origin
vertical axis (θ = π/2 ray) drawn as a full black line through the origin
origin/pole at intersection of the two axes
blue circle r = 2 centered at the origin, passing through (2,0), (0,2), (-2,0), (0,-2)
purple cardioid r = 2(1 + cos θ), cusp at the origin, rightmost point at (4,0), passing through (0,2) and (0,-2)
light-blue shaded region R: first-quadrant area outside the blue circle and inside the purple cardioid, bounded by θ = 0 on the right axis and closing at the point (0,2)
red radial line segment from the origin outward at an intermediate angle, crossing the circle and continuing to the cardioid
highlighted portion of the radial line between r = 2 (circle) and r = 2(1+cos θ) (cardioid) marking the representative radial strip
label 'r = 2' near the left side of the blue circle
label 'r = 2(1 + cos θ)' near the top right of the purple cardioid
label 'θ = π/2' next to the upper vertical axis
label 'θ = 0' next to the right horizontal axis
dynamic readout of the current θ and the inner/outer r-limits
marker dots where the red ray meets the circle and the cardioid
legend mapping blue = inner boundary, purple = outer boundary, light blue = region R

interactions.teaches: The outer boundary formula is what fixes the shape of R, where the two curves intersect, and therefore the upper limit of the inner r-integral.
interactions.label: Outer boundary r = f(θ)

interactions.teaches: Sweeping θ from 0 to π/2 shows that R is swept out by radial strips whose length 2(1+cos θ) − 2 shrinks to zero as θ reaches π/2.
interactions.label: θ (radial strip angle)

interactions.teaches: Seeing one strip alone versus the accumulated shading makes clear that the double integral adds up strip contributions over θ.
interactions.label: View

demo_steps.title: The two boundary curves
demo_steps.narration: The blue circle r = 2 and the purple cardioid r = 2(1 + cos θ) both pass through (0, 2) and the cardioid reaches out to r = 4 at θ = 0. In the first quadrant the cardioid lies outside the circle.

demo_steps.title: One radial strip
demo_steps.narration: Fix θ and follow the red ray outward: it enters R where r = 2 and leaves where r = 2(1 + cos θ). These are exactly the inner limits of integration.

demo_steps.title: The strip shrinks toward θ = π/2
demo_steps.narration: As θ increases the cardioid pulls in toward the circle, so the strip gets shorter and vanishes at θ = π/2, where both curves meet at r = 2.

demo_steps.title: Sweeping θ builds the region
demo_steps.narration: Sweep θ from 0 to π/2 and the strips accumulate into the shaded region R — the geometric meaning of the outer θ-limits.

demo_steps.title: Change the outer curve
demo_steps.narration: Edit the outer boundary formula and watch the intersection angle and region change: the limits of integration are read directly off the curves, not memorized.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The limits of a polar double integral are literally read off the picture: θ sweeps between the angles where the boundaries cross, and for each θ the ray enters R at the inner curve and exits at the outer curve.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Square canvas centered on the pole, with a thin black horizontal line (labeled 'θ = 0' at its right) and a thin black vertical line (labeled 'θ = π/2' at its top) crossing at the origin; scale so r = 4 fits comfortably. Draw the circle r = 2 as a thick sky-blue stroke and the cardioid r = 2(1+cos θ) as a thick purple/orchid stroke with its cusp exactly at the origin, bulging right to (4, 0) and symmetric about the horizontal axis; it crosses the circle at (0, ±2). Fill the first-quadrant lune between circle and cardioid with a pale translucent blue, leaving curve strokes visible on top. A thin red ray runs from the origin at roughly 45° out to the cardioid, with the segment inside R drawn heavier and small dots at r = 2 and r = 2(1+cos θ). Italic math labels: 'r = 2' to the left of the circle, 'r = 2(1 + cos θ)' above the upper-right of the cardioid. Show a small corner readout like 'θ = 0.79, r from 2.00 to 3.41'. A parse error in the equation field should appear inline near the field while the last valid curve stays drawn.
